text:
**What happened:** `origin/main` has commits that your local `main` doesn't contain, so your branch is not a descendant of the remote tip. Git refuses that push (non-fast-forward) because completing it would orphan the commits already on the remote. Someone pushed after your last fetch — or you rewrote local history (amend/rebase) and diverged that way.

**How to see which case you're in**, after `git fetch origin`:

```
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main    # commits on remote you don't have
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD    # your commits not yet pushed
```

If the first list is nonempty and the second contains only genuinely new work, it's a normal race. If the second list looks like rewritten copies of commits in the first, you rebased/amended something already published.

**What to do — normal case:** integrate the remote work, then push.

```
git pull --rebase origin main   # replays your commits on top of theirs
# resolve any conflicts, git rebase --continue, re-run tests
git push
```

Use `git pull --no-rebase` (a merge) instead if your local commits have already been pushed somewhere else or another person has branched off them — rebasing shared commits rewrites history other people hold.

**Do not** reach for `git push --force`; on this error it deletes the remote commits the hint is warning you about. If you legitimately need to overwrite after rebasing a branch that is only yours, `--force-with-lease` is the safer form — but never on `main`.

One note: if `main` is protected or shared by a team, the recurring fix is to stop committing directly to it — branch, push the branch, open a PR — which sidesteps this class of rejection entirely.
